Hoping to Sell Your Home in the Spring? It’s Not Looking Good
 
Plus, Nvidia’s Huang teeters, and a Megaspeed mystery
 

Good morning, I’m filling in for Spencer Jakab. Nvidia is raining on what just a day ago was a tech-stock parade. Shares in the chip giant are again falling on news the company is likely to oust CEO Jensen Huang over two extramarital affairs and a spy scandal. That threatens to erase a chunk of the gains Nasdaq racked up Wednesday following an upbeat quarterly report from neocloud CoreWeave. Futures for the Dow and S&P 500 are mixed, while moves in Treasury yields are so far muted following the Veterans Day break in trading.

 

​📈 Follow our live markets data and coverage.

11/12/2026, 6:13:21 AM ET
 
 
 

Build-a-bear

 

Here’s a disappointing sign for Americans hoping for better home-selling next year. Home builders are planning for a deep freeze in the spring. 

 

The number of new homes per community that builders started in October was 22% below September levels, data from John Burns Research and Consulting shows. Building slows at this time of year as part of the normal housing cycle, but this year’s drop is unusually large. Since 2012, the average seasonal decline in new housing starts from September to October has been 3%. 

 

Regular sellers can watch the housing market and list their property within days if conditions turn favorable—say, a drop in mortgage rates that gets buyers off the sidelines.

 

But builders have to make a call on what the market will look like in several months’ time. Large builders like Lennar or D.R. Horton need four to six months to build a home from scratch, so new-home starts in October reflect their expectations for the crucial spring-selling season. Almost 40% of new homes purchased every year in the U.S. are bought between February through May.    

 

“It is a telltale sign of how the industry is feeling right now,” says Rick Palacios, director of research at John Burns Research. “What we are seeing with home builders is a realization that spring 2027 is most likely going to be a repeat of 2026, if not slightly worse.”

 

One reason builders have hit the brakes: They already have a glut of completed, unsold homes on their hands. Demand from buyers has been so weak that builders have 50% more unsold homes per community than is normal for the time of year. 

 

Unsold inventory has also been rising in the existing-home market where sellers now far outnumber buyers. The National Association of Realtors will release existing-home sales data for October later today. The numbers reflect purchase contracts signed in late August and September, and are expected to be weak.

 

In September, worries about U.S. government debt sent yields on the 10-year Treasury above 5% for the first time since 2007. The bond-market move pushed the rate on a 30-year mortgage, which tracks the 10-year Treasury yield, above 7%.

 

Potential home buyers pulled back and mortgage applications fell. Hotter-than-expected inflation data released this week suggests relief from high mortgage rates isn’t coming soon. A big shift lower in rates would have to come soon to salvage next spring.

 

Owners who didn’t manage to sell their homes in the summer or fall will probably pull their listings over the winter and try their luck again early next year. Next time around, though, they may need to give ground on prices. That could mean even more pain is in store for the housing market.

Stocks I’m Watching

 

↘️ Nvidia: Shares in the company at the heart of the AI ecosystem tumbled premarket as investors braced for an exit of its totemic chief executive, Jensen Huang, following the revelation of two extramarital affairs.

 

↗️ Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom: Investors scrambled to process developments around Huang’s future. Nvidia’s competitors look like early beneficiaries. Shares in the chip makers rose by more than 3% premarket.

 

↘️ Sandisk, Micron Technology: Nvidia’s suppliers didn’t fare as well. Shares in the companies—which both count Nvidia among their most important customers—fell premarket.

 

↘️ CoreWeave, Oracle: Shares in the cloud-computing providers also fell premarket, reversing a rally in the last session. Nvidia has close financial ties to both CoreWeave and Oracle.

 

↗️ Burberry: Shares in the luxury retailer jumped over 8% in London after it posted better-than-expected sales. The result helped buoy European luxury stocks more broadly, with French bellwether LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton rising close to 2%.

 

↘️ Strategy: The bitcoin-hoarding group’s shares fell sharply premarket, after index provider MSCI said it would drop the stock from its global benchmarks at the end of the month.

One Big Chart

 
 
 
 

As recently as the summer of last year, Singapore was officially one of Nvidia’s biggest markets, generating 22% of the chip maker’s revenue. Then, practically overnight, it disappeared from the company’s financial disclosures.

 

Investors deserve to know why, and Nvidia needs to start explaining.

 

The timeline indicates that Nvidia altered its methodology for reporting the geographic breakdown of its revenue shortly after placing Megaspeed International on an internal block list. It isn’t clear if the two are related, but the shift had the effect of removing visibility into Nvidia’s sales tied to Singapore. That is the home to Megaspeed, the cloud-computing company embroiled in a sex-and-espionage scandal that has engulfed Nvidia and its chief executive, Jensen Huang.
